lessons.title: Send a signal
lessons.intro: A program is a precise instruction. Here, 7 is a number and .log() asks for it to be displayed.
lessons.goal: Read each part, then send the number 7.
lessons.result: The number 7 appears because the program explicitly displays it.
lessons.question: What does .log() do here?
lessons.remix: Make the program display 9 by replacing the blank.
lessons.remixHint: The value before .log() is the number to display.
lessons.independent: Write a program that displays 12. You may use any supported expression.
lessons.independentHint: Keep the display instruction and choose a value that gives 12.
lessons.learned: You connected a written instruction to its visible result.
lessons.answerHint: The value stays the same; .log() makes it visible.
answers: It displays the value before the dot.
It adds one to the number.
It stores a message on a blockchain.

lessons.title: Calculate a route
lessons.intro: An expression produces a value. The + sign adds two numbers; parentheses group the calculation before display.
lessons.result: The addition produces 5. The program displays that value.
lessons.question: Why is the output 5?
lessons.remix: Replace the blank so that (2 + ___).log() displays 8.
lessons.remixHint: Ask what number added to 2 makes 8.
lessons.independent: Display 11 using addition. Choose your own pair of numbers.
lessons.independentHint: Use + in the expression you display; several pairs will work.
lessons.learned: You used a calculation to produce a new value.
lessons.answerHint: + adds the numbers; the parentheses do not add a value.
answers: It adds 2 and 3 before displaying the result.
The parentheses add an extra point.

lessons.title: Give a value a name
lessons.intro: let n = 5; binds the name n to 5. Using n later refers to that value. The semicolon ends the declaration.
lessons.goal: Use the name n in a new calculation.
lessons.result: n refers to 5, so n + 2 produces 7.
lessons.question: Why does n + 2 produce 7?
lessons.remix: Change the declared number so that the program displays 10.
lessons.remixHint: The declared value plus 2 must equal 10.
lessons.independent: Declare a name with let, then use that name in an addition that displays 14.
lessons.independentHint: Choose a name and value, then add another number when you display it.
lessons.learned: You named a value and reused it in an expression.
lessons.answerHint: Reading n uses the value bound earlier. The addition does not rebind it.
answers: n refers to 5, so the calculation is 5 + 2.
The + sign changes n permanently to 7.

lessons.title: Fly to the next island
lessons.intro: A small plane needs to reach the next island. In this mission, the number your program displays becomes the number of spaces it flies.
lessons.goal: Calculate 2 + 3 and watch the plane fly five spaces.
lessons.result: The program displays 5. The game reads that output and makes a five-space flight; .log() itself still only displays a value.
lessons.question: Why is the output 5?
lessons.remix: Change the program to display 7 and reach the island seven spaces away.
lessons.remixHint: 2 plus the missing number must equal 7.
lessons.independent: Use addition to display 6 and land on the island six spaces away. Run and watch before submitting your answer.
lessons.independentHint: Choose two numbers whose sum is 6. You can also reuse a named value.
lessons.learned: You used a program’s output to control an action and checked the result.
lessons.answerHint: + adds the numbers; the parentheses do not add a value.
answers: It adds 2 and 3 before displaying the result.
The parentheses add an extra point.

guide.title: What is programming?
guide.text: Programming means describing a task with precise instructions. The computer follows the language rules; it does not guess your intention.
guide.takeaway: Here the goal is to display 7. Change the number and the displayed result changes.

guide.title: From text to action
guide.text: A compiler analyses text and translates it into a form a runtime can execute. This game's small interpreter first builds a structure, then evaluates it.
guide.takeaway: Meaning comes from structure: add first, then display. This game does not run the full Tolang compilation pipeline.

guide.title: Mistakes are clues
guide.text: Syntax rules describe valid shapes. A missing parenthesis breaks that shape. A valid program can still do the wrong thing: displaying 8 is valid, but it does not meet a goal of 9.
guide.takeaway: First make the program valid, then check whether its actual result meets the task.

guide.title: Why count work?
guide.text: Different instructions can produce the same result with different amounts of work. Computing and storing data use resources. The step count here is only a model for learning.
guide.takeaway: Both display 5. The second needs an addition. These counts cannot predict TVM gas or transaction fees.

guide.title: Tolang and a blockchain
guide.text: Tolang is used to write programs for ALUX. On a blockchain, changing shared state also involves transaction rules and agreement between nodes. Language and execution environment both matter.
guide.takeaway: Displaying a number in this game sends no blockchain transaction. These first ideas also help you learn other programming languages.

vault.title: The Vault Run
vault.intro: Three locks. One star core. Write the signals that open a path through the star bank.
vault.signalRule: Each .log() outputs one number. In this game, the vault reads those numbers in order.
vault.keyboard: Use English punctuation. New lines separate your instructions.
vault.consequence: Change a value, run again, and watch what reaches the receiver.
vault.allDone: All three mechanisms are open. Fresh clues let you try another solution; your stamps stay with you.
vault.meaning: let gives a value a name. + adds numbers. .log() sends the result to the output.
vault.practiceNote: Take your time: there is no countdown. Stamps record these game challenges, not programming mastery. Only the introductory number, addition and binding subset runs here.

vault.compare: The required output, in order, is {expected}. Compare it with what your program sent.

stages.title: The outer seal
stages.task: The lock needs the sum of A and B. Change the program so it sends that number.
stages.hint: Replace the 0 with B. Parentheses calculate first; .log() outputs the sum.
stages.learned: Your calculation became a signal the device could read.

stages.title: The energy gate
stages.task: Start with A energy and add B. Try giving the starting value a name, then use that name in the calculation.
stages.hint: let energy = A; stores A under the name energy. Use energy + B in the output.
stages.learned: A name lets you reuse a value without repeating it. Changing its binding changes later calculations.

stages.title: The core chamber
stages.task: Send three signals: A, then A + B, then A + B + C. The receiver reads exactly that order. Write the program yourself.
stages.hint: Use three .log() instructions. You can name A with let and reuse that name.
stages.learned: The same numbers in a different order produce a different result. Execution order is part of your program.
